analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using shared pricing software that fixes apartment rents.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for landlords to hire a third party — typically rent-setting software — that collects pricing, supply, and lease-renewal data from multiple landlords and recommends rents back to them. It declares this coordination a per se violation of the Sherman and Federal Trade Commission Acts, lets the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general sue, and lets any renter who was overcharged sue for triple damages with attorneys' fees. It also bars landlords from forcing tenants into pre-dispute arbitration over these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters — especially tenants in large apartment complexes where many landlords rely on the same pricing software — who currently pay rents set or nudged upward by algorithms fed with competitors' data. The bill gives them the right to sue for three times their overcharge plus attorney fees, and removes forced arbitration as an obstacle.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for any rental property owner to pay for the services of a 'coordinator' that collects pricing, supply, and lease-term data from two or more landlords and recommends rents back to them, deeming this a per se violation of the Sherman Act and an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act [S2].
It also outlaws performing the coordinating function itself, which directly targets rent-setting software companies that pool data from competing landlords and run a shared pricing algorithm [S2].

Any renter 'aggrieved by a violation' can sue for threefold damages plus attorney fees and litigation costs, and can invalidate pre-dispute arbitration agreements or class-action waivers that would otherwise block their claim [S2].

Enforcement is layered: the FTC may bring civil actions for penalties, the Attorney General enforces it as if it were part of the antitrust laws, and every state attorney general gets the same power [S2].

The bill covers all residential units — houses, apartments, accessory units, manufactured homes, and manufactured housing community lots — and does not preempt stronger state laws, so existing state protections remain in place [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, corporate landlords and the rent-setting software industry would bear the cost: they could no longer rely on pooled pricing algorithms, would face FTC and state enforcement and private treble-damage suits, and would lose the extra revenue that comes from coordinated rent recommendations. Some of that cost is exactly the inflated rents renters currently pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate landlords and rent-pricing software firms

drawbacks.text: The per se rule is unusually broad: it defines a 'coordinator' to include a rental property owner performing the coordinating function for its own benefit, so even a single large landlord analyzing its own portfolio's pricing data across units could face per se Sherman Act liability, a category normally reserved for outright cartels [S2].

Landlords and software firms argue that pricing software simply helps independent landlords price their units efficiently and that recommendations are not binding, so banning it could raise compliance and litigation costs that get passed through in a market where even lawful price-setting is already expensive — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2].

The bill does not cap rents or build new housing; it relies entirely on enforcement and lawsuits, so relief for any individual renter arrives slowly and only where a violation can be proven in court [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: renters in markets where many landlords feed the same algorithm pay measurably more than they would in genuine competition, and the bill attacks that mechanism directly with strong enforcement tools. The main cost is legal overreach risk — treating a landlord's internal pricing analysis the same as cartel conduct — and the possibility that some landlords abandon software that also produces legitimate, independent pricing. On balance the targeting is defensible, though the 'own benefit' definition invites litigation over ordinary portfolio management.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Becca Balint (D-VT) introduced the End Rent Fixing Act of 2025 on November 19, 2025, with 14 original cosponsors [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor action has occurred [S4].
36 House Democrats have cosponsored the bill as of the latest count [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. For now, the rent-setting software industry and large landlords keep operating under existing law, while renters await any relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Becca Balint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original cosponsors.

for.name: 36 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the House's Republican majority.

industries.industry: Rent-setting software providers (algorithmic pricing firms for landlords)
industries.note: Their core business — pooling pricing, supply, and lease-termination data from many landlords and recommending rents — is defined as an unlawful coordinating function, a per se Sherman Act violation, and they face FTC, DOJ, state AG, and private treble-damage suits. Their revenue comes directly from the coordinated rents tenants pay.

industries.industry: Large landlords and multifamily property owners
industries.note: They could no longer lawfully buy shared pricing recommendations, would face penalties and renter lawsuits for threefold damages, and would lose the above-market rents algorithmic coordination can produce. Some of what they lose is money currently extracted from tenants.

The bill applies to any rental property owner, so a small landlord using common pricing software could be swept in, but many also stand on the renter side of the ledger as consumers of the same housing market the bill aims to cool. The breadth of the 'coordinator' definition, which covers an owner analyzing its own data, is the main exposure.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled, and its cosponsors are exclusively Democrats in a chamber with a 223-seat Republican majority. Bills at this stage with this pattern of support overwhelmingly die in committee without a vote; unless the committee acts or the bill's rent-pricing provisions are attached to a larger package, it is likely to expire at the end of this Congress.
